content: Mefloquine is a medication used to treat and prevent malaria, a potentially fatal disease transmitted by mosquitoes in certain regions of the world. It belongs to a class of drugs known as antimalarials and works by killing the organisms responsible for causing malaria. Mefloquine is available in tablet form and is taken orally. For malaria prevention, it is typically taken once a week on the same day each week. Treatment should begin 1 to 3 weeks before traveling to a malaria-endemic area and continue for 4 weeks after leaving the area. If you are using mefloquine to treat malaria, your doctor will provide specific instructions on how often to take it. Always take mefloquine with food, preferably your main meal, and at least 8 ounces of water. Children may require smaller, more frequent doses. Follow the prescription label carefully and consult your doctor or pharmacist if you have any questions. Do not take more or less of the medication or take it more frequently than prescribed. The tablets can be swallowed whole or crushed and mixed with a liquid such as water, milk, or sugar water. If you vomit within 30 minutes of taking mefloquine, take another full dose. If vomiting occurs 30 to 60 minutes after taking the medication, take another half dose. If vomiting persists after taking the additional dose, contact your doctor. Mefloquine may also be prescribed for other uses. Consult your doctor or pharmacist for more information. Before taking mefloquine, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to mefloquine, chloroquine, hydroxychloroquine, quinidine, quinine, or any other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription medications, vitamins, nutritional supplements, and herbal products you are taking. Be sure to mention anticoagulants, antidepressants, antihistamines, calcium channel blockers, beta blockers, medications for diabetes, mental illness, seizures, or irregular heartbeat, as well as chloroquine, halofantrine, hydroxychloroquine, quinidine, and quinine. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication doses or monitor you closely for side effects. Inform your doctor if you have a history of mental illness (such as depression, anxiety, psychosis, or schizophrenia), seizures, or liver, heart, or eye disease. If you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, discuss this with your doctor. Use birth control while taking mefloquine, during your stay in a malaria-endemic area, and for 3 months after stopping the medication. If you become pregnant while taking mefloquine, contact your doctor. Do not breastfeed while taking this medication. Mefloquine may cause drowsiness and dizziness, which can persist after stopping the medication. Avoid driving or operating machinery until you know how the medication affects you. While mefloquine reduces the risk of malaria, it does not guarantee complete protection. Continue to take precautions against mosquito bites, such as wearing long sleeves and pants, using mosquito repellent, and sleeping under a bed net. The initial symptoms of malaria include fever, chills, muscle pain, and headaches. If you are taking mefloquine for prevention and develop these symptoms, contact your doctor immediately and inform them of your potential exposure to malaria. Plan ahead in case you experience severe side effects and need to stop taking mefloquine, especially if you are in a remote area without access to a doctor or pharmacy. You may need an alternative medication to protect against malaria or leave the malaria-endemic area. If you are taking mefloquine to treat malaria, your symptoms should improve within 48 to 72 hours after completing treatment. Contact your doctor if your symptoms do not improve. Avoid receiving any vaccinations without consulting your doctor, as they may recommend completing vaccinations 3 days before starting mefloquine. Prolonged use of mefloquine may damage your liver or eyes. Your doctor may recommend regular eye and liver function tests while taking this medication. Unless instructed otherwise by your doctor, continue your normal diet. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue your regular schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one. Mefloquine may cause side effects. Common side effects include upset stomach, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, loss of appetite, muscle pain, dizziness, loss of balance, ringing in the ears, headache, drowsiness, difficulty sleeping, and unusual dreams. If these symptoms are severe or persistent, inform your doctor. Serious side effects are rare but require immediate medical attention. These include tingling in the fingers or toes, difficulty walking, seizures, uncontrollable shaking, nervousness, extreme worry, depression, mood changes, panic attacks, forgetfulness, confusion, hallucinations, violent behavior, paranoia, suicidal thoughts, or rash. Mefloquine may cause other side effects, and some may persist after stopping the medication. Contact your doctor if you experience any unusual problems. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program. Store mefloquine in its original container, tightly closed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excess heat and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Dispose of expired or unneeded medication properly by consulting your pharmacist. In case of overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual collapses or is not breathing, call 911. Symptoms of overdose may include upset stomach, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, dizziness, loss of balance, headache, drowsiness, difficulty sleeping, unusual dreams, tingling in the fingers or toes, difficulty walking, seizures, or changes in mental health. Keep all appointments with your doctor and laboratory. Your doctor may order lab tests and periodic eye exams to monitor your response to mefloquine. Do not share your medication with others. Consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refilling your prescription.
